title: Code-switching few-shot play notes
content:
Quick brain-dump: experimenting with few-shot templates where examples mix English and Spanish (and occasional inline code). Reason: many end-users mix languages; models often hallucinate translations or drop context.

Goals:
- Find robust anchoring patterns so the model reliably follows bilingual examples (keep Spanish phrases as-is, only translate when asked).
- Measure token overhead and when bilingual shots hurt vs help.
- Capture clear failure modes to add to the prompt-library as negative exemplars.

Notes / hypotheses:
- Hypothesis 1: Explicit language tags per example (LANG: EN/ES) reduces accidental code-switching but adds tokens; tradeoff for safety.
- Hypothesis 2: Using short inline translations in parentheses (original — (en: ...)) helps but may bias answers toward translation-first.
- Hypothesis 3: Mixing languages inside the instruction ("Answer in the language of the question unless asked otherwise") + 2 bilingual exemplars = best balance.

Experiment matrix (keep simple):
- Template A: no tags, bilingual examples mixed naturally. 
- Template B: explicit tags per example: [LANG: ES] or [LANG: EN].
- Template C: anchor instruction + 2 bilingual examples + negative exemplar showing a bad translation.
- Variables: 1,2,3,4 shots; temperature 0.0, 0.7; model variant small/medium.

Small sample prompts tried (raw):
--- template A (2-shot) ---
Q: "¿Cuál es la mejor manera de empezar un newsletter?"
A: "Start with a clear hook and a short TL;DR. Example: \"Empieza con una pregunta que resuene...\""

Q: "How do I structure a technical note in Spanish?"
A: "Use an intro, code block, conclusion — include commands in English if they are code."

Instruction: "Answer the question in the language it was asked."

Observed failure: model sometimes answered first question entirely in English, then switched back to Spanish mid-answer. Token count for prompt: ~220 tokens.

--- template B (2-shot with tags) ---
[LANG: ES]
Q: "¿Cómo reducir el tamaño de una imagen en Linux?"
A: "Usa ImageMagick: convert input.png -resize 50% output.png"

[LANG: EN]
Q: "List best practices for API versioning"
A: "Use semantic versioning, maintain backwards compatible changes..."

Instruction: Follow language tag per example. Answer in the language of the question unless overridden.

Observed improvement: fewer unexpected switches. Downside: adds ~12 tokens per example. Also model sometimes printed the tag in its answer (e.g. "[LANG: ES] Para reducir..."). Need anchor to avoid echoing tags.

--- template C (2-shot + negative) ---
Example 1: [LANG: ES] Q: "¿Qué es un webhook?" A: "Un webhook es una llamada HTTP que..."
Example 2: [LANG: ES] Q: "Translate: 'rate limit' to Spanish" A: "límite de tasa"
Negative: [NEGATIVE] Q: "Translate: 'cache' to Spanish" A: "EN: cache (wrong)"
Instruction: Use positive examples and one negative to discourage one-to-one copy of English words.

Observed: shows reduced literal copies (e.g., "cache" less likely to be left in English). Negative exemplar helped but caused occasional disclaimers like "Note: negative example above is incorrect" — which leaks meta-instruction into output. Need to mask negative label better.

Failure cases logged:
- Model hallucinated that a user asked in English when prompt had Spanish examples first -> output entirely English. (happened at higher temp)
- Tags echoed verbatim in response (model repeating tag as part of answer)
- Negative exemplar triggered explanation mode instead of preventing behavior
- Code-containing answers occasionally got translated (e.g., code comments translated into Spanish unexpectedly)

Quick heuristics to try next:
- Put a compact metaprompt at the top: "System: For each query, detect language and answer in that language. Never restate language tags." (short, test token cost)
- Add an explicit 'DO NOT EXPLAIN EXAMPLES' line to prevent meta comments.
- Use binary anchors instead of text tags: Example header markers like "--ES--" "--EN--" (see if less repeated)
- Investigate tokenization: Spanish diacritics sometimes increase token counts; measure real impact with tokenizer.

Metrics to capture in spreadsheet (todo):
- Prompt tokens, response tokens, total cost estimate
- Language match accuracy (answer language equals question language)
- Fidelity (did answer respect domain constraints, e.g., did not translate code blocks)
- Echo rate (how often tags are echoed)
- Failure label (hallucination, switch, meta-explain, translate-code)

Practical quick tests to run (script):
- Run 200 samples across templates A/B/C at temp 0.0 and 0.7, record metrics above.
- Add a small test set of 40 user-style mixed-language queries collected from CS snippets (ask Diego for the list)

Notes to self / TODOs:
- [ ] Ask Diego for bilingual sample corpus (Slack: #prompt-lab thread id?)
- [ ] Add tokenizer stats per example (use tiktoken/our tokenizer)
- [ ] Try binary-anchor markers and measure echoing 
- [ ] Prototype a short "system" top-line and measure whether it reduces meta-explanations
- [ ] Add a negative-exemplar experiment where negative examples are only in a separate hidden slot (if runtime supports)

Random examples collected from runs (bad):
User: "¿Cómo hago un cron job?"
Model answer (bad): "To create a cron job, run crontab -e... Nota: this user asked in Spanish."
Notes: model appended meta note. Remove with explicit "DO NOT NOTE LANGUAGE" anchor.

References and links: see linked_artifacts above; also convo in Slack #prompt-lab 2024-11-10 (thread: code-switch experiments).

Rough notebook end — keep this as local scratch before formalizing into a template in prompt-library. Will convert the best template (likely B + system anchor) into a canonical entry if metrics show reliability > 96% language-match at temp 0.0.
